title: Taking The Ground Away
logline: On an upland slope where a sharp-leaved grass has taken the whole hillside and comes back within weeks of being cut or burnt, a plot is cleared the only way that lasts: the topsoil is forked open to two hands' depth and the mat of white underground runners is lifted out in slabs, shaken clean, carried off the plot and dried, because a piece the weight of a coin left in the ground will put the whole stand back.
human_question: What is the real difference between holding something down and taking away the place it could stand?

place.what_kind_of_place: Upland rain-fed country in the interior of the island's central east, on the dry side of the hills: broad open slopes at middling altitude, rock outcrops, scattered trees, small rainfed plots of maize and coarse grains cut into hillsides, a few tanks in the hollows, gravel roads, and long stretches of slope that are not cultivated at all and carry nothing but one grass. That grass is the subject. It is a tall sharp-leaved perennial that flowers in silver-white plumes, holds the great majority of its weight below ground rather than above it, and runs through the topsoil as a dense mat of pale jointed rhizomes with hard pointed tips that go through anything. Cut, it comes back. Burnt, it comes back faster and greener than before, which is why burnt ground reads as the youngest and brightest part of the slope. The working equipment is entirely hand tools and entirely blunt-force: a mammoty, a long-handled fork, a bar for prising, a sickle for taking the tops off first so there is something to see, a rake, and a basket or a tarpaulin for carrying the lifted mat off the plot. There is nothing to watch except the ground opening and the mat coming up, and nothing to judge by except whether a fork turns clean soil or catches another runner.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the slope is genuinely beautiful and the beauty is the concept. Wide and high, a hillside of this grass in flower is one of the most striking things in the island's interior: several hundred metres of silver-white plumes leaning the same way in the wind, with a few dark cultivated rectangles cut into it and the rock showing through in places. And the whole of that silver is the part that does not matter. Everything that decides whether the slope stays as it is lies under it, out of sight, and is a different colour and a different shape entirely. Close, the film is slow, heavy, unromantic work with an unusually clear test in it: the tops taken off with a sickle and raked aside, the fork driven in and levered, a slab of root-bound topsoil lifted out whole and turned over, and then the pale net of runners visible in it — flattened, jointed, branching, with growing points like small spears — shaken out of the soil by hand and thrown onto a heap. And the reason the heap has to leave the plot is the film's spine: a fragment of this thing the weight of a coin, left in the ground or turned back into it, is enough to start the entire stand again. So the job is not cutting a root. It is removing, piece by piece, every place the thing could stand.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The slope, on two clocks that do not match. On the short clock the plot changes completely in a few days: silver, then stubble, then opened ground, then a rectangle of clean red-brown earth with a drying heap of pale runners at its edge. On the long clock almost nothing changes at all, because the slope around the plot is exactly as it was, two feet away, and the boundary between the cleared ground and the standing grass is the whole argument of the film. The grass's own year runs against the work: it flowers and sets an enormous quantity of very light seed that travels on the wind, so a cleared plot is being re-seeded from the slope around it the entire time; and it comes away most cleanly when the soil is neither baked nor sodden, which is a short window after the first rains have softened the ground and before the plot has to be planted. The decision itself has a longer clock again. Taking the tops off is an afternoon and works until the next rain. Opening the ground and lifting the mat is days of the heaviest work available, for a benefit that shows up only in seasons nobody has reached yet, on land whose tenure may not be secure enough to make that a sensible thing to do.
place.when_it_looks_best: Two separate windows, and the film needs both. The slope wants the end of the dry season when the grass is in flower and the whole hillside is silver, filmed from height at first and last light, when the plumes catch and the surface of the slope moves as one thing; at noon the silver goes flat and grey and the slope reads as nothing. The work wants the short stretch after the first rains, when the soil has softened enough for a fork to go in and a slab to lift whole, which is also when it has to be done if the plot is to be planted. On the ground the digging wants the early morning and the late afternoon, because it is done in the open on an exposed slope and nobody works the middle of that day if they can help it. A burnt patch, filmed in the same light as an unburnt one, is worth a whole visit on its own.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about clearing one plot of one grass. A silver hillside at first light, moving in the wind; a small dark rectangle already cut into it; the tops taken off with a sickle and raked aside; a fork driven into the stubble and levered; a slab of root-bound soil lifted out and turned over to show the pale net inside it; hands shaking the runners out of the soil; a growing point held up, hard and pointed; a heap of pale roots carried off the plot on a tarpaulin and spread to dry; a burnt patch nearby already greener than anything around it; days of this, in the open, on a slope; and at the end a rectangle of clean earth with the silver standing two feet away on every side. It has a complete shape said out loud by nobody: the visible part removed, which does nothing, and then the invisible part removed, which is everything, and a heap that has to leave the ground because one piece of it is enough. Anyone who likes open upland country, heavy honest work, or the difference between a job done and a job finished has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same clearance becomes the distinction this whole group has been circling, in the source's own terms. The texts name three ways a harmful tendency can be got rid of, and they are not degrees of the same thing. It can be held down, which is what a settled mind does and which lasts while the settling lasts. It can be displaced for a time by its opposite. Or it can be cut off, and the texts are precise about what that means: what is removed is not a past state, which has already ceased, nor a future one, which does not yet exist, but the ground in which such a state could stand at all, so that it does not arise again. They add that the third only happens when calm and clear seeing are pulling exactly level, like two oxen of equal strength under one yoke, and that there is no shorter road to it than the graded one. A slope where the visible growth is irrelevant, where burning makes it worse, where the only lasting work is the removal of an underground mat, and where a fragment the weight of a coin is enough to undo all of it, carries that without anybody reciting it. The voice never says the grass is a defilement or that the plot is a person. It says this is the sources' own distinction, that the balance they describe is aimed at something no piece of work can reach, and that the analogy only holds for the ordinary graded part of the road.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high over an upland slope. Several hundred metres of tall grass in silver-white flower, all leaning the same way in the wind, with rock showing through and two or three small dark cultivated rectangles cut into it. The whole surface of the slope moving as one thing.
sequence.voice: Everything silver in this frame is the part that does not matter. Most of the weight of this grass is not in any of it. It is underneath, in a mat that runs through the top two hands of soil, and nothing that happens to the silver makes the slightest difference to that.

sequence.on_screen: Close: a sickle taking the tops off, the cut grass raked into a windrow. Then, in the same light, a patch burnt off some weeks ago, already greener and denser than anything around it. Then the stubble of the cut patch, with new blades coming through it.
sequence.voice: The books name three ways of getting rid of a thing, and they are careful that these are not three strengths of the same act. While the mind is settled, a settled mind presses the obstacles down and holds them there. Where clear seeing is strong, each insight displaces what it contradicts, for as long as it holds. And only when calm and clear seeing are pulling exactly level, like two oxen of equal strength yoked to one shaft with neither ahead of the other, does the third kind happen, which is cutting off [C016-P:L76]. Cutting the tops off is the first kind. Burning is the first kind done worse.

sequence.on_screen: The fork driven into the stubble and levered. A slab of root-bound topsoil lifted out whole and turned over, and inside it the pale net: flattened jointed runners, branching, with hard pointed growing tips. A hand shaking the soil out of it. The hole, and how deep it is.
sequence.voice: And the books are exact about what the third kind removes. A thing needs ground to stand on, they say, and where there is no ground it does not stand; in the same way a defilement needs a ground, and that ground is the aggregates themselves [C016-P:L78]. What is in them is what could arise if the conditions came; and what the path does is called the cessation by non-arising, which is to prevent them ever arising again [C016-P:L82]. Not the growth. The place the growth could happen.

sequence.on_screen: The lifted mat shaken out, gathered onto a tarpaulin, dragged to the plot boundary and spread in the sun. A single short fragment held up between two fingers — a joint, two nodes, nothing else. Then it is thrown onto the drying heap rather than dropped.
sequence.voice: This is why the heap has to leave the plot. A piece of this thing the weight of a coin will re-establish the whole stand. So the work is not one cut in the right place. It is going over the same ground again, and again, until a fork turns clean soil. The books say the same about the road they are describing: conduct first, then a settled mind, then nine great insight knowledges, and then the paths in order — and that no shorter way than that has been shown in this teaching [C016-P:L84].

sequence.on_screen: Two people on the slope through the middle of a day: one working fast and shallow, one slower and going deeper, then a stop, water, and both of them working at the same rate afterwards. Nobody correcting anybody out loud.
sequence.voice: The books are unusually practical about that balance. Strong steadiness with weak energy falls to the slack side and goes sluggish. Strong energy with weak steadiness falls to the other side and goes restless. Put the two exactly equal and the thing comes; and so, the text says, they should be made equal [C076-P:L661–L665]. The picture it gives is a driver who, once the horses are running level, stops correcting them at all [C076-P:L783]. And the balance itself is described as a kind of even looking that neither raises nor lowers any of the other factors [C076-P:L1328]. That is not a slogan about moderation. It is aimed at something a day's work cannot reach.

sequence.on_screen: The finished plot from height at the end of the day: a rectangle of clean red-brown earth, the drying heap of pale runners along one edge, and the silver standing two feet away on every side of it, coming right up to the line.
sequence.voice: Here is the limit of any comparison a film can make. The books count thirty-seven qualities on the side of awakening, and then say they reduce to fourteen real things, with one of them appearing in nine places under nine names and another in eight [C076-M:L109]. It is not a list to collect. And they say that while a person is working through the six ordinary purifications, only one of these can be had at a time — all of them arrive together only in the single moment of the path [C076-P:L1467]. So every human comparison, including this slope, holds only for the ordinary graded part.

sequence.on_screen: Last light from height. The whole hillside silver again, with the cleared rectangle a dark patch in it, small. Then the same frame going dark and the plumes losing their light.
sequence.voice: Two things this film is not saying. What the books are describing happens in one mind-moment, with the eight factors of the path arising together in a single consciousness that takes the unconditioned as its object [C016-P:L54], and no work with a fork resembles that, and nothing on this screen is it. And this is a decision about a grass. Whoever opened this ground did it for labour and for cost and because the plot has to be planted, and not one thing about it is a lesson, a virtue, or a verdict on anybody's land or anybody's year.

concept_merge.why_together: C016 supplies the distinction, the ground argument and the refusal of a short cut, and one line of it supplies all three at once. At C016-P:L76 the source maps the three abandonings onto three conditions of practice: where calm is strong, suppression; where clear seeing is strong, displacement by the opposite; and only where the two are pulling level, like two oxen of equal strength under one yoke with neither ahead, cutting off. At C016-P:L78 it argues that a defilement, like any object, needs a ground to stand on and cannot stand where there is none, and identifies that ground as the aggregates; at C016-P:L82 it names what has found that ground and defines what the path does as the cessation by non-arising, the prevention of its ever arising again. At C016-P:L84 it states flatly that conduct, then a settled mind, then the nine great insight knowledges, then the paths in order, is the whole road and that no shorter one has been shown. And at C016-P:L54 it gives the thing itself, eight path factors arising together in one consciousness with the unconditioned as object, which is the sentence that makes the film's closing refusal possible. C076 supplies the quality the work needs and, more importantly, the limit on the comparison. It pairs energy with steadiness and says that either one alone falls to its own side, sluggish or restless, and that they must be made equal [C076-P:L661–L665]; it gives the driver who stops correcting once the horses are running level [C076-P:L783]; it describes the balancing factor itself as an even looking that neither raises nor lowers any of the others [C076-P:L1328]; it reduces its own list of thirty-seven to fourteen realities, with one factor appearing in nine places and another in eight [C076-M:L109]; and it states that through the six ordinary purifications only one of these can be had at a time, all of them arriving together only at the path moment [C076-P:L1467]. A slope where the visible growth is irrelevant, where burning makes it worse, where the only lasting work is the removal of an underground mat to two hands' depth, and where a fragment the weight of a coin is enough to undo all of it, puts the ground argument and the three abandonings on screen in the same afternoon, and C076's last two citations are the only honest way to say out loud how far the comparison goes.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the difference the group has been circling is not a difference of degree, and that the harder option is rarely taken because its payoff is invisible at the time. Stated flat, suppression and cutting off sound like a weak version and a strong version of one act. Put on this slope they are two different jobs with two different objects: one deals with the growth, which is most of what you can see and almost none of what is there, and the other deals with the place the growth comes from, which you cannot see until you open the ground. The slope also supplies, free, the fact that makes the source's language exact rather than rhetorical: because a fragment is enough, the standard is not thoroughness but completeness, and 'so that it does not arise again' becomes a physical specification rather than a promise. The pairing keeps the film honest in the other direction too. C016 alone would turn a farm decision into a moral lesson about doing the hard thing, which is exactly what its digest and the group's floor forbid. C076 alone is advice about balance with nothing at stake, and its own digest warns that its balance is not a self-care slogan. Held together they make the film say two awkward things it would otherwise avoid: that the balance in question is aimed at something no day's work can reach, and that all thirty-seven of these qualities arrive together only in a single moment, so every human comparison — including this one — holds only for the graded ordinary part of the road. This idea keeps its concepts, its structure and both links from the previous pass; the changes are that the weed is now a specific one whose biology is the argument, that the farmer has been taken out of the centre so that the film is the digging and the root system rather than a character's decision, and that the closing beat now states the limit of the analogy out loud rather than leaving it to the risks.

concept_links.why: The film is this concept's distinction between holding down, displacing and cutting off, and its argument about the ground, and nothing else from it. The three abandonings are narrated over the cut tops and the burnt patch, in the source's own frame, where each is tied to a condition of practice and the third arrives only with calm and insight level, with the two oxen under one yoke given as the source's image [C016-P:L76]. The ground argument is narrated over the fork going in and the slab coming up: that a thing needs ground to stand on and does not stand where there is none, that the ground is the aggregates, and that what the path does is the cessation by non-arising [C016-P:L78; C016-P:L82]. The refusal of a short cut is narrated over the drying heap being carried off the plot, because that is the point at which the work is visibly going to have to be done again [C016-P:L84]. And the closing beat narrates the thing itself, eight path factors arising together in one consciousness with the unconditioned as object [C016-P:L54], precisely in order to say that no work with a fork resembles it and that nothing on screen is it. Every limit in the digest is honoured and two of them are on screen. 'Breakthrough moment' and 'life-changing epiphany' are refused by construction: there is no moment in this film, the work is days long, repetitive and unfinished at the end, and the narration states the graded road out loud. 'Everyone can be enlightened right now' is refused by the same citation. 'Good deeds will set you free' has no opening, since nothing in the film is framed as merit and no result in it is anybody's desert. The rebirth pathways, the seven lives, the pure abodes and the gender-specific route are all left out entirely, as the digest requires. No person is suggested, even by framing, to have reached any stage, and the closing beat says so. The digest's flagged uncertainties are all avoided: the count of forty supramundane absorption minds is not used; the probable typo at L54 is not quoted in Sinhala or paraphrased beyond what the line plainly says about the eight factors, one moment and the object; the internal tension at L126 and L190 about the once-returner path is not touched; the hundred-thousand-aeon claim at L62, the statement at L60 about merit in this era, the dry-insight claim at L110 and the gender-sensitive claim at L154 are all deliberately unused, since the digest says each needs an expert check. The lamp simile at C016-P:L56 and the treasure-house story at C016-P:L184 were read and are deliberately not narrated: both are images of a single flash of light doing several things at once, which pulls directly against a film whose subject is days of repeated heavy work, and the treasure-house additionally carries a night-to-sunrise arc that this slope cannot honestly supply. And the digest's own warning about this concept's story seed is respected: the film treats the clearance as a decision about labour, cost and a planting date, says so in its last line, and never presents it as a moral lesson.

This concept contributes the quality the work needs and, more importantly, the film's statement of how far its own analogy goes. The pairing of energy with steadiness is narrated over two people working the same slope at different rates: strong steadiness with weak energy falls to the slack side and goes sluggish, strong energy with weak steadiness goes restless, and the two are to be made equal [C076-P:L661–L665]. The source's own image of the driver who stops correcting once the horses are running level is spoken in the same beat [C076-P:L783], together with the definition of the balancing factor as an even looking that neither raises nor lowers any of the other factors [C076-P:L1328]. The limit beat narrates two of the concept's own statements about itself: that the thirty-seven reduce to fourteen realities, with one factor appearing in nine places and another in eight [C076-M:L109], and that through the six ordinary purifications only one of these can be had at a time, all of them arriving together only at the path moment [C076-P:L1467]. That second citation is the one the digest itself points to as the reason human analogies can only work for the gradual mundane stage, and the film says it out loud rather than relying on it silently. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured. 'Balance' is explicitly refused as a self-care or work-life slogan, in the narration, in the beat immediately after it is introduced. The 'do not stop even if flesh and blood dry up' framing of right effort is not quoted, so the film neither romanticises nor softens it. Mindfulness is not offered as stress relief or productivity, and no contemplation, body scheme or hindrance remedy from the concept is narrated. Equanimity is not filmed or narrated as indifference, and the definition used is the source's own engaged one. The thirty-seven are not presented as a checklist, which is what the reduction-to-fourteen citation is there to prevent. The four bases of success, the ministers' sons, the king's night walk, the raft of eight logs, the goldsmith and the two cautionary stories about monks who lost their attainments are all deliberately unused: the first three would cast real people as types, and the last two are monastic narratives the digest says must not become general moral tales about manual work or romance. Right livelihood and right action are not narrated, so nothing here reads as career advice. The concept's systematic OCR problem with the ද්ධ conjunct, and its long list of unclear or probably corrupted readings, affect none of the four lines quoted here, each of which was read in full and is plain.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That these texts distinguish three different things, not three strengths of one thing: holding a harmful tendency down, which lasts while the holding lasts; displacing it for a time with its opposite; and cutting it off, which they define not as removing a past or future state but as removing the ground in which such a state could stand, so that it does not arise again. That the third is said to happen only when calm and clear seeing are pulling exactly level, and that no shorter road than the graded one has been offered. And that the texts put a hard limit on comparisons of this kind, because the qualities involved arrive together only in a single moment whose object is the unconditioned, which is why the film says what it cannot show. The clearance is an analogy and the film says so. The decision on screen is about labour, cost and a planting date, and nothing about it is offered as a lesson or as a verdict on anybody.
what_must_be_real: The clearance as it would have been done anyway, on the plot it was going to be done on, at the time of year it is done. No ground is opened for the camera, no plot is chosen because it would look better, no runners are laid out, arranged or re-buried for a shot, no slab is lifted twice, and no burnt patch is burnt for the film. If the job is abandoned half done when something more urgent arrives, the film has that and keeps it; if the grass is back in the plot next season, the film says so and does not claim a success it has not seen. Nobody is asked to work faster, to work through the middle of the day, or to explain why they chose to dig rather than cut. No household's earnings, labour costs, credit or tenure is put on screen, and whether the plot is securely held is not investigated or implied, because tenure on upland ground of this kind is exactly the sort of thing a film can make trouble about. No household is named or followed as a character and the film has no protagonist. Nobody's endurance, strength or steadiness is filmed, cut or narrated as a spiritual quality, and the two people working at different rates are never compared.
position_hint: late in the group, immediately before or after the film about the change that cannot be watched, and after everything that establishes order and ground. It states in the plainest physical terms the distinction the whole group has been approaching, and it is the one film in the group whose single most beautiful shot is also the concept's flattest statement, which makes it a good place for the group to arrive at rather than to start from. It should not close the group, because it ends on a limit rather than on anything settled. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Treating a practical decision about labour, cost and a planting date as a moral lesson about doing the hard thing, which is the single most likely misreading and the one both digests name.
Letting the film imply that anybody who only cuts the tops has taken the lesser option. Cutting the tops is what most people do most years, for good reasons, and the film has no business judging it.
Presenting endurance, strength or patience on an exposed slope as a spiritual quality, or letting a rest in the middle of the day read as equanimity.
Taking a position on upland tenure or on land use, or filming in a way that could raise a question about whether a plot is securely held.
Overstating what one cleared plot proves. The standard the work is actually held to is that a fragment is enough, so nothing seen inside a filming window settles anything.
Letting 'balance' turn into a message about moderation or self-care, which the supporting concept's own digest refuses in as many words.
Letting the burnt patch read as a warning about fire, or the film drift into an argument about burning as a practice.
Sentimentalising the lifted root mat, or letting the killed stand stand in for a person's ending, which the group's floor rules out.
Making the silver slope decorative, so that the most beautiful footage in the film stops carrying the idea that everything visible is the part that does not matter.
Casting the two people working at different rates as energy and steadiness, which would turn them into props for a simile.
Attributing the young-tree-cut-before-fruiting image to this concept. It belongs to the account of the noble persons and is carried by another film in this group.
drop_if: Nobody is opening ground this way any more in reach of the filming window, because the job is now done with herbicide, and the film's central action would have to be commissioned.
No household will let a real clearance be filmed on its own terms, at its own pace, without the order or the timing being adjusted.
Filming would require the plot's tenure to be established, or would expose a household to a question about it.
The only plots available are on land this slate is committed to staying off, or in a crop carried elsewhere.
The slope's flowering window and the digging window cannot both be reached, so the film loses either its widest shot or its whole action.

connections.note: Both are about the removal of a ground rather than of a growth: one inside a closed heap where nobody can see it, one lifted out of a slope in slabs where everybody can.
The same distinction asked of a person's life rather than of a slope, which is the question this film deliberately refuses to answer.
One film about a sequence that can always be taken one step finer, and one about a job whose standard is that nothing at all may be left.

selection.reason: The concept's own distinction is this slope's physical fact: the visible growth is irrelevant, burning makes it worse, and because a fragment the weight of a coin restores the whole stand, 'so that it does not arise again' is a specification rather than a figure of speech.

review.note: Kept 2026-09-24 with both concepts, both links and the argument unchanged, and rebuilt around a specific grass whose biology is the concept rather than around a farmer's decision. The previous version had an unnamed deep-rooted weed and a farmer choosing, one year, to dig rather than cut; the choice made the film a character study and put a household's reasoning at the centre, which the group's floor and both digests warn against. The film is now the digging and the root system: the tops coming off, the fork going in, the mat of underground runners lifted out in slabs, the heap carried off the plot, and the cleared rectangle with the untouched slope two feet away. Three facts about this particular grass do the work the previous version had to assert. Most of its weight is below ground rather than above it, so the widest and most beautiful shot in the film is of the part that does not matter. It regenerates faster after burning or cutting than before, so the first of the source's three abandonings has a visible counter-example on the same slope. And it re-establishes from a rhizome fragment of about a tenth of a gram, which turns the source's phrase 'so that it does not arise again' into a physical specification and is why the lifted mat has to leave the plot. Both digests were re-read as a new reader and every citation was re-tested line by line against the source files. Of the previous pass's two citations, C076-P:L783 survives re-testing and is kept; C016-P:L76–L82 has been split into the three separate lines that actually carry the argument, because L76 carries the three abandonings and the two oxen, L78 carries the ground argument, and L82 carries the cessation by non-arising, and citing them as a range obscured which line says what. New to this pass: C016-P:L84 for the refusal of a short cut, C016-P:L54 for the closing statement of what cannot be shown, C076-P:L661–L665 for the pairing of energy with steadiness, C076-P:L1328 for the definition of the balancing factor, C076-M:L109 for the reduction of thirty-seven to fourteen, and C076-P:L1467 for the statement that all thirty-seven arrive together only at the path moment, which is the line that lets the film say out loud how far its own analogy goes. The digest's warning that the young-tree-cut-before-fruiting image belongs to the account of the noble persons and not to this concept has been honoured twice over: it is not attributed here, it is carried by another film in this group under the concept that owns it, and a risk has been added so that it is not re-introduced later. The lamp simile and the treasure-house story, both available in this concept's extract, were read and are deliberately unused, because both are images of one flash of light doing several things at once and would pull against a film whose subject is days of repeated heavy work.

suggested_location.name: The upland rain-fed plots and open grass slopes of the Kandaketiya division, in the interior of the Badulla District

also_known_as.name: illuk
also_known_as.meaning: the grass the whole film is about, recorded botanically as Imperata cylindrica and in English as cogon, blady or spear grass; the name is in ordinary Sinhala use for it

also_known_as.name: illuk mul
also_known_as.meaning: the underground runners themselves, which are what has to be lifted out; a reported and ordinary compound rather than a technical term, and its use in this district has not been checked
also_known_as.used_by: reported Sinhala usage, unverified for this district

also_known_as.name: udu goda
also_known_as.meaning: the upland part of a holding, as against the paddy in the hollow; the plots the film is about are on the upland side

suggested_location.region: Badulla District, Uva Province: the interior uplands in the north of the district, on open middling-altitude slopes of rainfed maize, coarse grains and scrub, well below and well away from the district's plantation country
suggested_location.why_here: Because the grass and the farming system that produces it are both documented in this kind of country, and because this particular division is upland rainfed smallholding rather than plantation. The grass is recorded as one of the most dominant and difficult weeds of the humid and sub-humid tropics of Asia, as holding the large majority of its biomass below ground, as regenerating vigorously from rhizome after cutting or burning, and as re-establishing from fragments of about a tenth of a gram; the literature also links its grasslands specifically to repeatedly burnt and shifted cultivation ground, which is what large parts of this country are. Forking the rhizomes out to about forty-five centimetres is recorded from an island trial as giving long-lasting control, which is the operation the film is built on. The division itself is identified in the department of agriculture's own extension arrangements as upland country where maize is a main crop, with thousands of hectares of upland and tens of thousands of farm families in the wider extension area, which is the scale the film needs: small plots, hand tools, and slopes that are not worth mechanising. It is inland, obscure, on no tourist route, and deliberately chosen away from the district's plantation belt and away from every named place this slate has already claimed. And the slope gives the film its one indispensable shot for nothing, because a hillside of this grass in flower is silver from end to end and all of it is the part that does not matter.
what_to_film: The slope in flower from height at first and last light, so the plumes catch and the whole surface moves as one thing, and again at noon when the silver goes flat and grey.
The boundary between a cleared plot and the standing grass, from directly above, held still: a dark rectangle with silver coming right up to the line on every side.
The tops taken off with a sickle and raked into a windrow, at arm's length and without emphasis.
A patch burnt off some weeks earlier, filmed in the same light as an unburnt one, greener and denser than anything around it.
The fork going in and being levered, and a slab of root-bound topsoil lifted out whole and turned over, in one unbroken take if it can be got.
The pale net inside the slab at close range: the flattened jointed runners, the branching, the hard pointed growing tips, and a hand shaking the soil out of it.
One short fragment held up between two fingers, then thrown onto the heap rather than dropped, which is the smallest and most important action in the film.
The heap gathered onto a tarpaulin, dragged to the plot boundary and spread to dry.
The open hole and its depth, measured against a tool handle or a hand rather than against a ruler.
Two people working the same slope at different rates in a single wide frame, with the stop and the water, and never in cut-together close-ups.
The finished plot at the end of the day from height, and the same plot again a season later if the film can get back, whatever it shows.
suggested_location.access: By road inland from the district's northern approaches and then on gravel and farm tracks; the plots are private smallholdings on open slopes, so everything depends on the household whose plot this is agreeing, and on being introduced through the divisional agriculture office or a farmer organisation they already deal with rather than cold. The film needs two separate windows — the slope in flower at the end of the dry season, and the digging in the short stretch after the first rains when the soil will give up a slab whole — so it is two visits and not one, and the second one is triggered by rain rather than booked. The work is done on exposed slopes and stops in the heat of the day, so the crew has to be able to work the same hours and not ask for others. The hazards are the ordinary ones of the country: sun and no shade, loose ground on a slope, hand tools swung near feet, and the grass itself, whose leaf edges and root tips cut. Drone flight over occupied smallholdings needs the household's agreement whatever the general position is. The wider district is plantation country and it would be easy to drift into it from the roads; the film has to stay on the upland smallholding side, which is a matter of where the crew is taken rather than of where it can go.
suggested_location.best_time: Two windows in one year. First, the end of the dry season, when the grass is in flower and the slope is silver, for the elevated and wide material, at first and last light. Second, the short stretch after the first rains have softened the ground and before the plot has to be planted, for the whole of the work, in the early morning and late afternoon. A third short visit a season later is worth planning for and may be the most important one in the film, because whether the grass is back is the only real test of anything shown and cannot be arranged.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. On the grass, from the invasive-species and weed sources above: Imperata cylindrica is among the most dominant, competitive and difficult weeds of the humid and sub-humid tropics of Asia, West Africa and Latin America; the majority of its biomass is below ground, given as more than sixty per cent of the total; it spreads by rhizomes that descend deep into the soil; a high root-rhizome to shoot ratio gives it a large source of regeneration after cutting or burning; it succeeds particularly on ground that is frequently burnt, overgrazed or intensively cultivated; and it reproduces asexually from rhizome fragments as small as about a tenth of a gram. Its common Sinhala name is illuk. The formation of grasslands of this species is linked in the literature to repeatedly logged and burnt land under shifting cultivation. The forking-out figure the film depends on comes from a nineteen-seventies paper comparing manual and chemical control of this species in Sri Lanka, which reports that forking out the rhizomes to a depth of about forty-five centimetres gave long-lasting control; that trial was conducted on tea land, and the film has nothing to do with tea, so the figure is taken as evidence about the plant and the operation and not about the setting. On the place: the division named is a divisional secretariat of this district, and the department of agriculture's inter-provincial extension arrangements identify it as upland country in which maize is a main crop, within a wider extension area recorded as having thousands of hectares of upland and tens of thousands of farm families. The single largest assumption in this record is that forking the rhizome mat out by hand is still done here at all, rather than the job being done with herbicide or simply not done; that is the first thing to check on the ground. Three further things the film depends on are inferences about this division: that slopes of this grass in flower of the scale described are present and reachable, that a clearance will fall inside a filming window, and that the soil-moisture window in which a slab lifts whole is as short as assumed. The coordinates are a published position for the division and are a direction towards the country the film needs, not a survey: no slope, plot, household, organisation or officer has been identified or approached, and no permission has been sought from anybody. No photograph of this district's slopes, of any clearance or of a lifted rhizome mat was found on Wikimedia Commons; the one image is of the species in flower, photographed elsewhere.

unknowns: Whether the rhizome mat is still forked out by hand in this division at all, or whether the job is now done with herbicide or left undone, which would remove the film's central action.
How deep the work actually goes here, and whether the forty-five centimetre figure from an island trial on other land describes what is done on these slopes.
Whether the lifted mat is in fact carried off the plot and dried, which is the beat the whole argument turns on, or whether it is turned back in.
How short the window really is between the soil softening enough for a slab to lift whole and the plot having to be planted.
Whether slopes of this grass in flower of the scale the widest shot needs are present and reachable in this division.
Whether a household will let a real clearance be filmed at its own pace and on its own plot, without the order or the timing being adjusted, and on whose introduction.
Whether the film can return a season later to see whether the grass is back, which is the only real test of anything it shows.
Whether height can be obtained over these slopes, and whether the boundary between cleared ground and standing grass reads from the air as strongly as it should.
